texts.text: The first weekend of that month I took the long route up the ridge alone, something I had wanted to do for years and kept postponing. The morning was clear. By the time I reached the shoulder of the hill it was not, and the cloud came down so completely that the cairns disappeared one by one until I was standing on a slope of wet rock with no idea which direction was down. I waited. I ate the second sandwich. I counted to a hundred several times for no reason I can defend. After an hour or so the cloud thinned enough to show a line of fence posts, and I followed them to a track and the track to the car, and I sat in the driver's seat for a long time before I turned the key. I do not know how to file that day as either good or bad. The hour on the rock was the loneliest I had spent in a decade, and the view when it finally opened was the finest I have ever seen, and I would not trade one for the other. What that day taught me is that waiting is a skill and not a failure, and that a place can frighten you and still be worth going back to. I went back in the autumn. The cairns were all there, exactly where they had been the whole time.

spans.meaning: What that day taught me is that waiting is a skill and not a failure, and that a place can frighten you and still be worth going back to.

texts.text:
I don't want to write this and I'm going to anyway.

Driving my nephew back from his swimming lesson this afternoon, a van came through the junction and hit the back passenger side. The side he was sitting on. The car spun half round and stopped against the kerb. For a few seconds nothing made any sense, and then I heard him crying, which was the best sound in the world because it meant he was awake and breathing.

He is fine. They checked him over for three hours and he is fine, bruised along the arm where the belt held him, and already telling everyone at home about the fire engine. I am fine, apparently.

I keep going over it, and the thing I keep arriving at is this: I was the one in the driver's seat. I was the adult he was handed over to, the one who was supposed to get him home. That is where I was in all of this, and that is where I will be in it whenever my sister looks at me for the next while.

And the other thing, which I need to say plainly: the van driver did this. He came through without stopping, the witness said so, the marks on the road say so. It was not me. I was doing nothing wrong. He did this.

I still hate that it happened on my watch. I hate that it was my car and my afternoon and my nephew in the back.

No more tonight.

texts.text:
Small, odd day. Nothing to report except the kettle. It stopped working mid-boil this morning and I spent forty minutes taking the base apart with a butter knife before admitting it was dead and walking to the shop for a new one. My partner found this funny. I found it a bit funny and a bit annoying, in roughly equal halves.

A few notes since I'm here anyway. My shoulders were tight the whole time I was crouched over it, which I only noticed because I kept rolling them. It was my fault it broke, probably, I've been overfilling it for months and the manual says not to. And I'm aware that I'm the one in this house who has to try to fix things before I'll let anyone buy a replacement; that's just the seat I sit in. I've always been like that about frustration, I keep a lid on it and go quiet and fiddle with screws rather than say out loud that I'm annoyed. Partner knows this, makes tea in a saucepan, and waits.

What I learned, if a kettle can teach anything, is that forty minutes is my limit before I'll admit defeat. I'm writing it down so I can check that number next time something breaks, that's all this entry is for.

New kettle is blue. It's fine. Day was fine.

Quick one. I finally got the sourdough to rise properly. Fourth attempt, and this time it actually came out of the oven looking like the pictures, with the ear and the open crumb and the whole business. Ate half of it with butter, standing at the counter, still warm.

What it taught me is that the slow way is the right way with this; leave it alone overnight and it does the work by itself. I'd been poking at it every hour on the earlier attempts like it owed me something.

It has also, honestly, changed my whole weekend. Nothing is the same about Saturday mornings now; there's a thing to check on, a thing to shape, a reason to be up and about before nine with the radio on. I like it more than I expected to.

I'm noting the overnight trick here so I remember to do it next time rather than reading six forum threads again. That's the only point of this entry.

Loaf: good. Toast tomorrow: better. Mood: good.

texts.text:
My sister came round tonight. She didn't text first, she just turned up with a bag of oranges and the nephew's drawing of the fire engine, and stood in the hall until I let her in.

We talked for four hours. Four. I don't think we've done that since we were teenagers sharing a room. She said she had been angry for about a day and then had sat with it and was not angry anymore, and that she had needed to come and say that to my face rather than over the phone. Then she asked how I was, and waited, and actually listened to the answer.

Somewhere around the second hour I noticed my shoulders had come down from around my ears and my chest had gone loose and warm, the way it does after a hot bath. I hadn't realised how tightly I'd been holding everything for nine days.

I want to be fair about this: the credit is hers. She made the first move, she walked over here, she chose the oranges and the drawing. I was still hiding behind one-line texts. Whatever happened tonight happened because she decided it would.

What it means, I think, is that the two of us are still a family that repairs things, even now, even when it's hard.

She left at midnight and hugged me in the doorway for a long time. The nephew's drawing is on the fridge, slightly crooked, held up with the magnet shaped like a lemon.

Session 6. Client arrived on time, presentation flat but engaged. Session focused on a minor interpersonal event from the past week: a friend cancelled a planned coffee for the second time this month by text, approximately an hour beforehand.

Client described irritation and a low mood that lasted the rest of the evening, which they rated as mild and noted had passed by the following morning. Client was clear that the event itself was "small" and "not the point".

Client attributed the cancellation to the friend's chronic disorganisation rather than to any change in the friendship, stating, "She's like this with everyone, it isn't about me." Clinician noted that this differs from the self-blaming attributions reported in earlier sessions.

Client described their position in this friendship, and in most friendships, as "the one who does the chasing, the one who books the table and sends the reminder". Client expressed some fatigue with this role but no wish to change it at present.

Client offered the following self-description: "I get clingy when people go quiet. I always have. Even a two-hour delay in replying and I'm checking my phone every few minutes." Clinician noted the pattern as consistent with themes raised at intake.

When asked what the episode meant to them, client stated, "What it tells me is that I can be annoyed at a friend without it turning into a crisis about whether they still like me." Clinician affirmed this.

Plan: continue monitoring attribution style in low-stakes interpersonal events. Homework: notice one instance of waiting for a reply without checking. Next session as scheduled.

texts.text: There was a Sunday that month we drove out to the coast, the two of us, because the week had been dull and we wanted a horizon. It was, in short, a disappointing day, and not one I would otherwise have remembered. The sea was the colour of dishwater and the café we liked had changed hands and now served everything in paper, and the walk along the front was shorter and shabbier than either of us recalled. We sat in the car for a while with the heater on and watched a dog refuse to go into the water. On the drive home we were quiet, not bickering, just flat, the way you are when an outing has not paid out and nobody wants to be the first to say so. It would have been forgotten entirely except for a small thought I had on the motorway, which has outlasted the day itself: what I took from that Sunday is that the places I loved at twenty-five are not obliged to stay the same for me, and that going back to check is a kind of tax I will keep paying anyway. The dog never did go in. We did not stop for chips. We were home before dark, which felt like the final insult.

spans.meaning: what I took from that Sunday is that the places I loved at twenty-five are not obliged to stay the same for me, and that going back to check is a kind of tax I will keep paying anyway.

texts.text:
They packed a bag tonight. Not everything, a bag. Said they needed a few weeks at their brother's to think, and that it wasn't a decision, it was a pause, and that they would call on the weekend. Then the door, and the car, and the sound of the car getting smaller.

I'm not going to try to make sense of it tonight. I'm not going to go back through the last six months looking for the place it started. I know I will do that eventually and I know I'll do it badly, and I want to not do it yet.

What I will do is put down exactly what was said, because in a week this will have softened or hardened in my head, and I want the true version to exist somewhere. That's what this entry is for. Not to process. To keep.

They said: "I love you and I don't know if I'm happy." They said: "This isn't a leaving." They said: "Please don't text tonight." They took the grey jumper and the book from the bedside and the good pillow. They left their keys on the hook, which could mean they're coming back or could mean nothing at all.

The flat is very large. The fridge is making the noise it makes. I've left the hall light on, which is stupid, and I'm not going to turn it off.

I haven't texted.

spans.function: I want the true version to exist somewhere. That's what this entry is for. Not to process. To keep.

texts.text:
PASSED.

Writing it in capitals because I shouted it in capitals. Opened the email on the stairs and read the number three times and then made a noise I don't think I've ever made and sat down right there on the step, because my knees actually went, a proper wobble, and my face was hot for about ten minutes after.

Twelve marks over. Not scraping. Twelve.

I rang my sister first. She screamed. The nephew screamed because she was screaming. Then I rang my manager, who said "I knew it", which he did not, but it was nice of him.

Here's what I want to say while it's fresh. I earned this one. Not luck, not an easy paper. Me, at the kitchen table, every evening for five weeks with the lamp on and the phone in the other room. Nobody else did those evenings. I did.

And I'm not the one who passes anymore. That version got broken in the winter and I'm glad, because the one I am now is the one who failed and came back. That's a better seat to sit in. I like it better here.

This is the line, I think. There's before this email and there's after it, and I can already feel that I'm going to count things from today.

Going out for dinner with my sister. Sparkling water, and I don't even mind.

texts.text:
Ran into someone from the old flat today, in the queue at the pharmacy of all places. I hadn't seen her in five years. The last time we spoke I was supposed to be at her father's funeral and I was not, and I never explained, and I never answered the three messages she sent afterwards.

She said my name first. I almost pretended not to hear.

We ended up in the café next door for an hour. I told her the truth about that year, all of it, the parts I'd never said out loud to anyone. She listened. She didn't let me off. She said it had hurt, a lot, and that she had spent a long time wondering why. Then she said she was glad I'd said it now, and asked how long I'd been sober, and I told her, and she said "good" and squeezed my hand across the table.

I don't know what we are now. We swapped numbers. We said the thing people say about coffee.

Walking home I felt two things at once and I'm still feeling both. The first is relief, plain relief, like putting down a bag I'd carried so long I'd stopped noticing the weight. The second is the plain old shame, not smaller, just finally out in the open where she could see it too.

I'm glad it was the pharmacy. I'm glad there was a queue. I'm glad she said my name before I could decide whether to say hers.

texts.text:
Grey day. Nothing in it.

The train was late, then it was crowded, then it stopped outside the station for twenty minutes with nobody saying why. Work was the same spreadsheet as yesterday and will be the same spreadsheet tomorrow. Lunch was a sandwich eaten at the desk. Somebody's birthday cake in the kitchen, the kind with the thick icing; I had a slice and didn't want it.

There was a dull ache behind my eyes from about two o'clock onward, the kind that doesn't become anything but doesn't go either, and my neck was stiff from the train, and by the time I got home I had the tired-but-not-sleepy thing where you lie on the sofa and can't be bothered to reach for the remote.

Ate toast for dinner. Talked to nobody. Looked at the hall light for a while.

A nothing day, and a low one. I'll have forgotten it by the weekend, which is fine.

Bed.

Session 12. Client arrived slightly late, apologised, settled quickly. Affect notably more animated than in recent sessions, with some tearfulness toward the end.

Session was given almost entirely to the client's account of a three-day walking trip taken alone over the long weekend, which client had booked some weeks ago and had considered cancelling. Client described the trip as "the biggest thing that's happened to me in months, and I'm not sure if it was good".

Client described the first evening in the hostel as very difficult: "my stomach was knotted up the whole evening, I couldn't eat the dinner I'd paid for, and I lay there with my jaw clenched listening to other people laughing downstairs". On the second day, on the hill, client reported the knot loosening by mid-morning and "not coming back". Client described the summit as "quiet, enormous, and I cried for about ten minutes and didn't mind".

Client was asked what the trip meant to them. Client stated: "What it taught me is that I can be on my own and be all right. Not happy, necessarily. All right." Client became tearful here and clinician allowed silence.

Client stated unprompted that they want to hold on to this memory for a specific reason: "I want to keep it so that next time I'm dreading an empty weekend I can point at it and say, you did three days, you were fine. It's evidence. That's what it's for." Clinician affirmed the use of concrete experience as counter-evidence.

Client declined to discuss partner contact this session. Mood: mixed, with pride and grief both present and both named by client. Plan: revisit next session; continue sleep diary.

texts.text:
Session 13. Client arrived early and began speaking before sitting down. Affect labile across the session, moving between flat and animated. Client stated at the outset that they had "news" and wished to use the whole session on it.

Client reported that their partner returned to the flat at the weekend, by arrangement, for a conversation about the pause begun several weeks ago. Client described the conversation as lasting most of an afternoon and ending with an agreement to separate. Client reported that the partner will collect the remainder of their belongings over the coming fortnight and that both parties have agreed to a period of no contact afterwards.

Client was notably clear about their own role in the conversation. Client stated: "I'm the one who said it. Not them. I was the one who put it on the table and said we should stop, and I want to be clear about that." Client returned to this framing several times and appeared to draw some steadiness from it.

Client described the week since as "grief and relief taking turns, sometimes within the same hour". Client reported sleeping better than expected and also being unexpectedly upset in the supermarket. Client did not seek to resolve the two feelings into one and clinician did not encourage this.

Client stated: "This is the hinge. Whatever my life looks like from here, it is not going to look like the one I had before Sunday. Everything is going to date from that afternoon." Clinician reflected the weight of this and client agreed.

Client did not offer an account of why the relationship ended and clinician did not pursue this today. Plan: hold space for the separation process; review support network next session; continue sleep diary.

Session 14. Client on time. Mood described as "fine, a bit fed up". Client did not wish to return to the separation this week and instead spent the first part of the session on a minor recreational disappointment, which clinician accepted as a reasonable use of the time.

Tuesday nights are going to be something else from now on, I just don't know what yet." Clinician reflected the finality of this and client confirmed it, with some humour.

Client asked that the episode be noted in the record "so that when I next mention a class someone's recommended, you can remind me about the kneeling". Clinician agreed.

texts.text:
They offered me the lead on the new programme today. Not the deputy, not "supporting". The lead. The director took me into the small meeting room, the one with the broken blind, and said it in about four sentences, and then asked if I wanted to think about it, and I said no, I don't need to think about it, yes.

I said yes. Out loud, first time, no hedging.

I've sat in a lot of rooms in that building. I've been the one who takes the notes, the one who passes, the one who failed and came back. From today I'm the one they turn to when the question is hard. That's my chair now. I keep looking at the phrase and it still fits.

I know what I'd normally do with news like this. I'd fold it up small and put it away and tell people "oh, it's just a title" for a month until the shine wore off. I've always been like that with good feeling, I keep it on a short lead so it can't get away from me and so nobody can take it. I'm trying not to do that tonight. I'm trying to let it be as big as it is.

Rang my sister. She said "about time". The nephew asked if I was the boss of everybody and I said nearly.

This one's a line in the sand. There was my working life up to this afternoon and there's whatever starts on Monday, and they are not the same thing, and I'm glad.

No wine. Didn't even cross my mind until I wrote that sentence, which is its own kind of news.

texts.text:
She came to dinner. The friend from the pharmacy queue, from the old flat, from the funeral I didn't go to. I cooked the only thing I can cook for guests and she brought a bottle of the posh elderflower stuff without me having to say anything, which told me she'd been listening in the café.

It was easy. That's the astonishing thing. I'd braced for three hours of careful, and instead we were twenty minutes in and laughing about the landlord from the old place and the time the bath came through the ceiling. She had photos on her phone from that year, ones I'd never seen, and in one of them I'm asleep on the kitchen floor with a colander on my head and she's pointing at me and howling.

We talked about her dad. Properly. I asked about the funeral and she told me, and I listened, and at one point she stopped and said "you're allowed to ask, you know", and I said thank you.

She left at eleven. Hugged me in the doorway, and the hug was the old kind, the kind where you lean.

What it means, I think, is that some things can be mended even after a very long time, and that the mending doesn't have to be dramatic to be real. It can be a casserole and a colander photo. That's enough. That counts.

I washed up slowly. I didn't want the evening to be over yet, so I made it last another twenty minutes with the taps running and the radio low.

texts.text:
Sunday lunch at my sister's. Roast, slightly overdone, as always, and nobody minded, as always.

The nephew made me read the dinosaur book four times. I'm the one in this family who does the voices; my sister refuses on principle and her husband does them all in the same voice, which the nephew finds unacceptable. So it's me. The stegosaurus has a cold. The big one with the teeth is from the north. I've been doing these voices for three years and I will apparently be doing them until he's twelve.

After lunch I lay on their sofa with the sun coming through the big window straight onto my legs and had that heavy, warm, full-stomached feeling where your eyelids weigh about a kilo each. I dozed for twenty minutes with the nephew's feet in my ribs. Woke up to the smell of coffee and someone laughing in the kitchen.

We did the crossword, badly. My sister got the long one. I got the one about rivers, which she pointed out was "my corner". It is.

Drove home with the windows down and the radio on something I didn't recognise and didn't mind.

Nothing happened today. It was nice. That's all.

texts.text:
Lido this evening. Shouldn't have bothered.

The water was the coldest it's been all year and the lane was full of people doing butterfly badly, and I got kicked twice, and by the second length my fingers had gone white and I couldn't feel my feet at all, just a sort of distant thudding where they should be. Got out after six lengths. Sat in the changing room with my teeth going and my skin stinging all over as the blood came back and thought, why do I do this.

I'm the one who organises these. For four years I've been the lido person in our little group, the one who sends the "anyone fancy a swim" message and books the slot and brings the spare towel. Everyone else drifted off ages ago. It's just been me and the message for most of this year, and tonight it was just me and the message and a stranger's heel in my shoulder.

Well. That was the last one. I mean it this time. The lido era is over; something else will go in that slot on Thursdays and it is not going to involve a changing room. Decided, on the bench, with the teeth going. I'm not going to miss it, or I'll miss the idea of it and not the thing itself.

Bad evening. Tea, hot bath, bed.

Client reported that earlier in the week they had sent a colleague a sharp, one-line email during a busy afternoon, and had felt uncomfortable about it for the rest of the day. Client described their role in the office in relation to this: "I'm the one in that office who says sorry first. If there's friction, I'm the person who goes over and clears it." Client stated this without apparent distress and with some pride.

Clinician asked what the client made of the episode. Client stated: "What it tells me is that the gap between doing something I'm not proud of and putting it right can be about eighteen hours, and that the putting-right is usually smaller than the dread. That's it, really."

Client was explicit that this was a minor event and that they did not want to over-read it. Clinician agreed and did not extend the discussion.

Remainder of session on support network mapping and a brief check-in on the separation, which client described as "proceeding". Mood: positive, settled. Risk: none identified. Plan: next session as scheduled.

month_summaries.summary: Four things, if I'm honest about what this month actually was. The day on the ridge when the cloud came down and I stood on wet rock for an hour not knowing which way was down, and then the view opened and I have never seen anything like it; I still don't know whether to call that day good or bad, and I've stopped trying. The afternoon the van hit the car with my nephew in the back seat, and the three hours waiting while they checked him over, and the plain fact that it happened on my watch. Then the email that said I hadn't passed, two marks short, and having to walk into an office full of people who knew I'd sat it and say nothing. And my sister turning up at the door with a bag of oranges and a drawing of a fire engine, and four hours of talking, and the feeling of my shoulders finally coming down from around my ears. Everything else this month was weather. Those four were the month.

This month had a hundred days in it, and a wedding where I sat with sparkling water and a slice of lime and for the first time didn't explain myself to anyone; I woke the next morning with steady hands and knew something had turned. Three days later my partner packed a bag and went to their brother's for "a pause", and I wrote down exactly what they said so I wouldn't rewrite it, and I didn't text. Then the resit result, twelve marks over, read on the stairs, shouted down the phone to my sister, the first thing in a long time I could say I'd earned outright. And at the end of the month, in a pharmacy queue of all places, the friend I'd disappeared on five years ago said my name, and I sat with her for an hour and finally told her the truth, and walked home carrying relief and shame at the same time and not knowing which was heavier. A hundred days, a bag by the door, an email, a queue. That was the month.

Three days alone on the hills at the start of the month, nearly cancelled, a knot in my stomach the whole first night in the hostel and then, on the second morning, gone; I cried on the summit and didn't mind, and I came down knowing I could be on my own and be all right. A week later the conversation with my partner that ended it, by agreement, in our own kitchen, and I was the one who said it, and everything since dates from that afternoon. Then the director in the small room with the broken blind offering me the lead, and me saying yes without hedging, and trying for once to let good news be as big as it actually is instead of folding it away. And the next evening my old friend at my table, a bottle of elderflower, photos from the old flat with a colander on my head, the kind of hug where you lean. Grief, pride, a chair, a mended thing. That's what mattered this month.
